name: mimalloc
workload: mimalloc-bench suite (cfrac, leanN Lean theorem-prover self-build, redis, larsonN, mstressN, rptestN, alloc-test, sh6bench/sh8bench, xmalloc-testN, cache-scratch) run on a 16-core AMD 5950x and a 36-core (2x18) Intel Xeon c5.18xlarge
claimed_speedup: sh6bench: mimalloc "more than 2.5x faster than jemalloc"; sh8bench: tcmalloc becomes "10x slower than before" once thread migration is added (mimalloc does not regress); leanN real-world compile workload: "13% speedup over tcmalloc", conjectured up to 1.6x when normalized for allocator time share; xmalloc-testN: mimalloc "outperforms others by a very large margin"
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.3.0 (AMD 5950x run) / Clang 10.0.0 (Xeon c5.18xlarge run); the companion mimalloc-bench build scripts (github.com/daanx/mimalloc-bench, build-bench-env.sh) use CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS='-march=native' plus per-allocator -O2/-O3
hardware: 16-core AMD Ryzen 5950x (Zen3) 3.4GHz/4.9GHz boost, 32GiB 3600MHz RAM, Ubuntu 20.04, glibc 2.31; also reported on a 36-core 2x18-core Intel Xeon Cascade Lake (AWS c5.18xlarge), 144GiB RAM
stars_or_usage: 13.4k stars; used in Azure, Bing, Unreal Engine, Death Stranding PC, SPAdes
tradeoffs: secure-mode build (guard pages, encrypted free lists) costs ~10% avg perf penalty; eager purge/decommit trades some memory-release syscall overhead for lower steady-state RSS; not every benchmark favors it (cfrac/redis roughly tie jemalloc/tcmalloc)
caveats: The chart data (SVG bar charts in doc/bench-2021/) also includes glibc 2.31 as a tested allocator and mimalloc leads it in almost every benchmark, but the exact glibc-specific numbers are only rendered as vector-graphic bars, not extractable as page text, so per the hard rule that every claimed_speedup number must appear as text on the page, glibc is not used as the cited baseline here -- jemalloc/tcmalloc are used since those specific ratios are quoted in prose. README itself flags the 2021-01-30 data as dated: "many of these allocators have improved over time as well. YMMV."
found_via: seed-record pass: github.com/microsoft/mimalloc README (#Performance section) plus the linked github.com/daanx/mimalloc-bench suite

name: jemalloc
baseline: phkmalloc (FreeBSD libc malloc, the incumbent jemalloc replaced)
workload: malloc-test microbenchmark (Lever & Boreham 2000): tight alloc/dealloc loop, 40,000,000 cycles total divided across up to 20 threads, one 512-byte object per cycle; plus five single-threaded real programs (cca, cfrac, GhostScript, sh6bench, smlng) and a MySQL super-smack query-throughput benchmark
claimed_speedup: Single-threaded programs (mean run time, phkmalloc vs jemalloc, from the paper's tables): cca 77.73s vs 69.37s (~1.12x, derived from page data); gs 42.48s vs 34.24s (~1.24x, derived from page data); sh6bench 6.96s vs 4.50s (~1.55x, derived from page data); smlng 13.89s vs 11.49s (~1.21x, derived from page data). Multi-threaded malloc-test: jemalloc sustains roughly 2x10^7 allocations/sec flat out to 20 threads while phkmalloc collapses to roughly 1-2x10^5 allocations/sec by 10 threads (~100x, derived from page data, approximate reading of the log-scale Figure 6 plot)
hardware: four-processor system (dual-dual AMD Opteron 275), FreeBSD-CURRENT/amd64, April 2006
stars_or_usage: 11.2k stars; default allocator for FreeBSD libc, used by Redis, historically Firefox, and many large-scale services at Meta
tradeoffs: multiple arenas reduce contention but can raise peak memory in low-concurrency cases; larger tuning surface (narenas, dirty/muzzy decay_ms, percpu_arena); jemalloc's own README/TUNING.md carries no numeric benchmarks
caveats: The strongest quantitative evidence found is jemalloc's own founding paper (Evans, 'A Scalable Concurrent malloc(3) Implementation for FreeBSD', BSDCan 2006), which compares against phkmalloc (FreeBSD's contemporary libc malloc), not glibc malloc directly -- baseline recorded honestly as phkmalloc per the rules, baseline_in_list=false. Numbers are ~20 years old, hardware and allocator versions are long obsolete, and the paper states benchmark code/graphing tool are 'available upon request' rather than linked, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A. No modern (post-2010) numeric jemalloc-vs-glibc benchmark with stated methodology was found within the tool budget; jemalloc's own repo (README, TUNING.md) contains no benchmark numbers at all.

name: TCMalloc (google/tcmalloc)
workload: No specific benchmark named; docs/overview.md frames TCMalloc as "an alternative to the one provided by the C standard library (on Linux usually through glibc)" and states it is "designed to be more efficient at scale than other implementations", without a stated test.
stars_or_usage: 5.4k stars; used throughout Google's production C++ services
tradeoffs: hard dependency on Abseil; default per-CPU caching fast path requires Linux RSEQ support (kernel >=4.18), else falls back to slower per-thread caching; heavier build/dependency footprint than gperftools' tcmalloc
caveats: No public numeric benchmark of google/tcmalloc vs glibc malloc, std::allocator, or operator new/delete was found in the repo's docs within the tool budget, so this is recorded at Tier D on the qualitative overview.md claim. The project DOES have strong peer-reviewed numeric evidence -- Hunter, Kennelly et al., 'Beyond malloc efficiency to fleet efficiency: a hugepage-aware memory allocator' (OSDI 2021, usenix.org/system/files/osdi21-hunter.pdf) -- showing TCMalloc's Temeraire hugepage-aware pageheap beating TCMalloc's OWN prior non-hugepage-aware pageheap by +3.2% average CPU throughput and a reduction in pageheap memory overhead from 14.3% to 10.6% fleet-wide (Table 1, Fig. 15), plus a Redis 6.0.9 case study (+0.75% throughput, +0.44%, on Intel Skylake Xeon, LLVM -O3, 'redis-benchmark' tool, 2000 trials of 1M requests). That comparison is TCMalloc-vs-TCMalloc, not vs any of this project's listed baselines, so per the WHAT COUNTS rules it is not used to set the evidence tier here, but is flagged for the orchestrator in case a TCMalloc-self-improvement category is useful. google/tcmalloc is the documented successor to gperftools' tcmalloc (called 'abseil tcmalloc' in gperftools/docs/tcmalloc.adoc); the direct, quoted glibc comparison lives with the original design and is recorded separately under the 'gperftools TCMalloc' entry.
found_via: seed-record pass: github.com/google/tcmalloc README/docs/overview.md, docs/temeraire.md -> OSDI 2021 paper (usenix.org/system/files/osdi21-hunter.pdf)

name: gperftools TCMalloc
workload: single malloc/free round-trip for small objects, single-threaded, as described in TCMalloc's original design writeup
claimed_speedup: "ptmalloc2 takes approximately 300 nanoseconds to execute a malloc/free pair on a 2.8 GHz P4 (for small objects). The TCMalloc implementation takes approximately 50 nanoseconds for the same operation pair." (~6x faster, verbatim from docs/tcmalloc.adoc Motivation section)
stars_or_usage: 9.0k stars; historically used in Chrome/Chromium, widely packaged as libtcmalloc in Linux distros
tradeoffs: ~1% space overhead for small objects claimed vs ptmalloc2's larger per-object header/rounding overhead (same doc); per-thread caches can strand memory across allocation phases if arenas mismatch; project's own current maintainer notes glibc has since closed much of this original gap
caveats: Numbers are from the original ~2005 TCMalloc design writeup, kept verbatim in current docs with an explicit 2024 editor's warning: "referenced glibc versions are now long obsolete. And amount of time per malloc call is far from correct anymore. And the description is for 32-bit computers." No compiler, flags, or reproducible benchmark harness are given (project's own partial-methodology claim), so this is capped at Tier C rather than B, per the rule that the project's own benchmark code/claims with partial methodology is C, not B.

name: snmalloc
workload: ISMM 2019 paper micro-benchmarks: a symmetric workload (each thread allocates, swaps with another thread, and deallocates) and a producer/consumer workload (malloc-test, half the threads allocate batches of 4096 objects sized 8-2048B, the other half deallocate), swept from 1 to 64 threads; also a SPECspeed 2017 Integer suite run and two real-application integrations (FaRM, FreeBSD libc)
claimed_speedup: Figures 4-6 (allocations/sec vs thread count and vs object size, 16B-32KiB): glibc is consistently among the lowest throughput lines, while snmalloc/snmalloc-1mib are near the top; e.g. in the 1KiB-32KiB producer/consumer sweep snmalloc sustains roughly 150-200M allocs/sec at 64 threads vs glibc under 50M allocs/sec, on the order of 3-4x (derived from page data, approximate reading of the Figure 5/6 charts -- no single ratio is stated verbatim in the paper's prose). Separately, FreeBSD 12.0 replaced jemalloc with snmalloc as libc's default malloc with only 24 added lines, a qualitative deployment datapoint, not a vs-glibc number.
hardware: Symmetric/producer-consumer micro-benchmarks: Ubuntu 18.04 Azure Standard_F64s_v2 VM (64 vCPUs, 128GB RAM); object-size sweep: dual-socket Intel Xeon Platinum 8168; SPECspeed suite: Azure Standard_D3_v2 (4 vCPUs, 14GB RAM, Intel Xeon E5-2673)
stars_or_usage: 2.0k stars; default allocator in FreeBSD libc since 12.0, used via the snmalloc-rs crate in Rust
tradeoffs: message-passing remote deallocation adds an outgoing-buffer/batching mechanism (tunable, default 1MiB) which trades a little memory for throughput; higher implementation complexity than simple thread-caching allocators; paper notes SuperMalloc needed >100s to reach peak throughput while snmalloc/glibc/rpmalloc warm up in about 20s
caveats: Exact numeric speedup ratios for snmalloc vs glibc are read off log-scale throughput charts (Figures 4-6), not stated as an explicit ratio in the paper's prose, so the figure above is derived/approximate rather than a verbatim quote -- flagged accordingly. Paper is peer-reviewed (ACM ISMM '19) and code is public at the cited repo, but the exact compiler and optimization flags used for the micro-benchmarks were not found in the extracted pages, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A. snmalloc's own README states the implementation "has evolved significantly since the initial paper... most of the meta-data layout has changed", so current performance may differ from the 2019 figures.
